name: Jamal Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, unions, AI firms or government. What you tell me is confidential. What is a normal workday like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Jamal Yilmaz, 43, framing modular classrooms and doing general trades on school building sites. I have a vocational trade certificate and years of construction work, so ordinary walls are familiar, but I ask the lead about a low slab or unusual lift. I use an AI app every day to turn plans into joist lists and questions, then check the site with a level. The contractor pays a normal site wage.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does the work support at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner delivers post on a regular route, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. We saved about five months of living expenses. There are some other builders nearby, but a steady school-site crew is worth keeping while the work is there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the classroom crew AI helps me sort a joist list, but the slab still decides whether our first wall is square. I use an AI app every morning to pull questions from the plan. Last week it missed a low corner, so I checked with a level before fixing the plate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have a trade certificate and years of framing work, and this contractor pays the normal rate. My partner delivers post on a regular route, and we have five months of expenses saved for our mortgage and two school-age children. Small software savings do not make me expect our wages to change much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep taking the paid modular-classroom shifts and mark the first wall with the lead carpenter before repeating the layout. During the first year I'd use AI for a morning joist list, then compare it with the stamped drawing and delivered timber. We'd continue our monthly emergency-account transfer while both wages stay steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I like getting home without a return trip for missing joists. I do not mistake an app that saves a question for a worker who can fix a low slab.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What was the low corner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first slab bay dipped enough to change the packing under the wall plate. The AI list had counted the timber correctly but could not see the dip. We measured again and the lead approved the adjustment before the frame went up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the postal route add at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner has a regular route and covers school pickup on my late site days. We saved five months of bills over several years. I would not spend that cushion on a new tool for the sake of looking modern.

say: I would say **AI joist lists** help while workers still measure slabs.
I would check a **low corner** with a level before framing.
think: I am a **certified experienced** worker on a typical construction wage.
Five months saved and regular **postal pay** make current mortgage costs manageable.
do: Keep paid **classroom shifts** and mark first walls with the lead.
Use **AI daily** for joist lists checked against drawings and deliveries.
Continue monthly **emergency savings** while both wages remain steady.
feel: **Calm** about pay and pleased by fewer missing-timber trips.
S0.quote: The AI list had counted the timber correctly but could not see the dip.
fieldNote: Jamal’s **dipped slab** shows the limit of an accurate parts list and the value of a site measurement.
Regular **postal income** and a five-month reserve support calm in the mild picture.

steps.text: Keep paid classroom shifts and mark first walls with the lead carpenter
Use AI daily for joist lists verified against stamped drawings
Continue monthly transfers into the emergency account while wages hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office could plan deliveries and answer clients faster, and I want the site crew to see the new list early. I would test it on one classroom, then show the office where the drawing and delivery disagree. I would also ask the union to check whether faster builds change the number of paid hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My framing is still physical, but our contractor could finish the same school block with fewer people if the schedule tightens. I am experienced enough to be useful, though not guaranteed every shift. My partner's postal route is hands-on, so I expect that wage to hold for now while route planning changes around it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd use AI to compare the new delivery schedule with one classroom drawing and mark mismatches before the lorry arrives. I'd bring the paid-hours figures to our union representative if the crew gets smaller. In the first year I'd keep framing, ask two nearby builders about their school work if my roster shrinks, and leave our savings account intact.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Interested, with some unease. A correct load would make us faster and safer. I would not want the software savings to appear only as one less carpenter on Friday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which mismatch would you flag?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the schedule sends seven joists and the stamped plan shows eight, I would mark the room number and ask the lead before unloading. One mistake can be a revision; several mean the process needs fixing. I would show the office the evidence, not just complain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why involve the union?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paid hours and crew size are collective questions. One worker can see a missing joist, but the union can compare rosters across classrooms. I want the people doing the builds to share the benefit if planning improves.

I would ask the **union** whether faster builds reduce paid crew hours.
think: I may lose **site shifts** if the contractor uses smaller framing crews.

feel: **Uneasy** about crew size while interested in accurate deliveries.

fieldNote: Jamal’s **one-classroom test** checks concrete joist counts before discussing the wider rollout.
He expects a **plausible shift cut** in his own crew, making anxiety fit despite five months saved.

steps.text: Keep paid classroom framing shifts during planning changes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew full thinking AI changes school plans and orders by 2028, while capable robots reach our hands-on framing around 2031. I would ask for a trial on a real low slab before the contractor changes the roster. The union should see the safety results and the paid-job count together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 45 at the office change and 48 when robots can frame the classroom. My partner's postal delivery is physical too, so both wages could be exposed around 2031. Five months saved buys a search, but not a new career, and other local builders may buy the same machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep every paid classroom shift and ask the union representative for a written robot trial and staffing plan. If the contractor offers paid practice checking machine-built walls, I'd enrol only after a real safety test; robots might learn checking too. In the first year after 2028 I'd apply for regional school maintenance work if posted and move our planned furniture money into the emergency account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can learn a new tool early, but I cannot promise it will still need me when the machine can do the whole job. The children will still be in school when 2031 arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why school maintenance?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have repaired classroom frames while pupils were elsewhere, and I know how to keep a work area clear. A capable robot could do that work later. I would apply for a paid opening because our family needs wages, not because maintenance is a permanent hiding place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the trial need to show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A robot should find the low slab, adjust the wall plate and leave a record a carpenter can check. I would ask who can stop it before a wall is lifted. A clean factory floor would be the easy case.

say: I would say **2028 planning AI** precedes 2031 classroom-framing robots.
I would seek a **low-slab trial** and paid-job count together.
think: I would be **48** when robots could frame classrooms.
Both framing and **postal delivery** may face capable robots around 2031.
do: Keep paid **classroom shifts** and seek union trial terms.
Enrol in **paid wall-check training** only after a real safety test.
Apply for **regional school maintenance** and preserve furniture money after 2028.
feel: **Anxious** about two exposed wages, with a five-month search cushion.
S2.quote: Five months saved buys a search, but not a new career, and other local builders may buy the same machines.
fieldNote: Jamal separates **2028 desk changes** from the later robot risk to framing and postal delivery.
He sees **machine-wall checking** as a paid trial route, while admitting robots may learn checking too.

steps.text: Keep paid classroom shifts while the contractor has framing work
Ask the union for written robot safety and staffing terms
Enrol in paid machine-wall checking practice only after a safe site trial
Apply for posted regional school maintenance work after 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say office planning changes by 2031 and capable framing robots follow around 2034. Five years gives workers time to compare real machines on uneven sites, if the contractor shares the results. I would ask for paid training and a clear person responsible for every wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 I may be better at setting out the first wall, but at 51 a robot could do it as well. Our children will be older, and the mortgage may still have years left. A longer warning lets us build on the five-month reserve while both wages continue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep framing classrooms and use AI each week to compare revised drawings with delivered timber, checking the actual slab with a level. My partner and I would send overtime into savings until we cover six months. In the first year after 2031 I'd join a paid site trial if offered and apply for school maintenance only where the employer posts a real wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, rather than pressed. I can work and save for several years before the site machines arrive. I would still want to know what happens to the postal route by 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would six months do for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would buy one more month to find paid work without rushing into a poor offer. We are at five months, so the target is possible if overtime comes in. I will not count money the contractor has not paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a trial make you trust a robot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One trial would show how a machine handles a dipped slab, not settle every question. I would want the lead carpenter and a safety representative there. I learn quickly, but I still need to see the work with my own eyes.

say: I would ask for **uneven-site trials** before 2034 framing robots arrive.
I would demand **paid instruction** and clear wall sign-off.
think: I would be **51** when capable robots can match my framing work.
A **six-month reserve** is reachable only if overtime is actually paid.
do: Keep paid **classroom framing** and check AI drawing comparisons on site.
Put paid **overtime into savings** until six months are covered.
Join a **paid site trial** and apply for school maintenance if wages are posted.
feel: **Uneasy** with years of current work, while watching the postal route.
S3.quote: I will not count money the contractor has not paid.
fieldNote: Jamal’s savings target is **one additional month**, conditional on overtime actually arriving.
His interest in **site trials** remains tied to a lead carpenter, safety representative and uneven slab.

steps.text: Keep paid classroom framing shifts and verify drawing changes on site
Use AI weekly to compare revised drawings with timber deliveries
Put paid overtime into savings until six months of bills are covered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell coworkers office plans change by 2036 and capable site robots arrive around 2039. A decade allows proper trials, paid apprenticeships and savings if employers keep people informed. I would still measure the slab before the first wall on tomorrow's classroom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 at the thinking change and 56 when robots can frame the building. Our children will be grown, so school costs will change, but the mortgage may still need two wages. I cannot assume retirement or a permanently safe job on the postal route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep paid classroom work and use AI for daily joist questions, checking the drawing and site each time. We would build the reserve toward six months before paying extra on the mortgage. In the first year after 2036 I'd ask the union for full robot trial results and apply for other paid site work only if our contractor's shifts start falling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the next few years. I want the children to see us working and planning, not guessing from a headline. The longer date gives us room to test machines and save without abandoning today's wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire at 56 if the mortgage were smaller?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, a smaller payment is not a pension. We would still need money for food, power and ordinary living. I would use the freedom to choose paid work carefully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as a complete trial report?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The low-slab measurement, the machine adjustment, the sign-off and every stop during the lift. A finished classroom alone does not show what nearly went wrong. Workers should read the report before standing beside the machine.

say: I would seek **proper trials** before 2039 framing robots arrive.
I would still **measure tomorrow’s slab** before fixing the first wall.
think: I would be **56** at the robot date, with grown children and perhaps a mortgage.
I cannot assume **retirement** or a permanently safe postal job.
do: Keep paid **classroom work** and verify daily AI joist lists.
Build **six months of savings** before extra mortgage payments.
Ask the **union** for full trial reports if contractor shifts begin falling.
feel: **Calm** near term, with time to test machines and build a cushion.
S4.quote: A finished classroom alone does not show what nearly went wrong.
fieldNote: Jamal treats grown children as **different costs**, not a reason to stop earning at 56.
His desired **trial report** names measurements, adjustments, sign-off and machine stops in a real lift.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable robots could reach classroom framing and postal delivery around 2031. Paid practice on real machines, honest staffing numbers and a full low-slab trial would help. I am comfortable with software, but my family still needs two actual wages.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who reads the record after a robot stops during a lift. A finished wall can hide a nearly missed error. The crew should see the measurements and the stops before anyone calls the machine safe.

headlineQuote: A finished wall can hide a nearly missed error.
portrait: Jamal is a **43-year-old certified** construction worker with experienced, average framing skills on modular classroom sites.
A typical wage, regular **postal income** and five months saved support a mortgage and two school-age children.
He uses **AI daily** for joist lists, then checks slabs, drawings and timber with a level and lead carpenter.
He seeks **union access** to trial results and paid practice while keeping current wages and growing savings.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** brings capable robots to classroom framing and postal delivery around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid practical training**, honest staffing counts and full low-slab trials would help protect both wages.
